column3:
1. Hospitals forecast their monthly need for each medicine and send requests.
2. Warehouses deliver stock to pharmacies (chain, independent, hospital).
3. Patients buy medicines in-store or online (e-commerce). The POS records price, discount, prescription, payer and payment.
4. Some sales are returned, and online orders can be 'returned to sender'.
5. Problem: POS, e-commerce and hospital ERP data sit in separate systems at different detail (per sale vs per month), so there is no single view of demand.
Scope: 63 medicines, 7 disease areas, 60 pharmacies, 12 hospitals, 500K sales, 2023–2025.

column1:
How are your competitors faring?
(those with and without DWH)
column3:
Our competitors:
• Medicine makers: Pfizer, Novartis, GSK
• Medicine distributors: Cardinal Health, Cencora
• Pharmacy chains: CVS, Walgreens

With DWH:
• Walgreens – one data platform forecasts demand and moves medicines between ~9,000 stores. Saved millions in supply-chain cost and raised planning productivity by 20%.
• Pfizer – moved its 20-year-old data warehouse to a modern cloud platform (Snowflake). Some data processing dropped from hours to minutes.
• CVS Health – building a Google Cloud data platform to join data from 9,000+ pharmacies and 1,000+ clinics (launching 2026).
• Adamed (pharma) – Azure DWH + Power BI. Demand forecast error is below 5%.

Without DWH:
• Depend on Excel and separate POS reports -> slow reports (Walgreens' old setup took 48 hours to make store data usable), wrong forecasts, stockouts in one place and excess stock in another.

column1: List and Summarize Case Studies with Successful DWH solutions
column3:
International:

1. Walgreens (USA, pharmacy chain)
Problem: Store data took 48 hours to become usable, so demand planning was slow.
Solution: One data platform (Databricks) joining store, pharmacy and supply data.
Result: Forecasts demand and moves medicines between ~9,000 stores. Saved millions in supply-chain cost and raised planner productivity by 20%.

2. Fortune-500 pharma company (USA, by phData)
Problem: Demand planning was done manually in Excel.
Solution: Moved it into a Snowflake DWH with Power BI reports.
Result: 24-month demand forecast and one shared view of demand and stock for all teams.

3. Adamed (Poland, pharma)
Problem: Forecasting was manual.
Solution: Azure DWH + Azure ML + Power BI, pulling marketing, CRM and product data together.
Result: Fully automated monthly forecasts for 18 months ahead, with error below 5%.

Local (Pakistan):

4. Martin Dow (Pakistani pharma company)
Problem: Company data was spread across many systems.
Solution: Built its own BI platform "Genesis" on SAP BW/4HANA (a data warehouse).
Result: Over 80% of company data in one place. 9 dashboards used daily by management, real-time reports, and predictive planning for production and supply chain.

column1:
What are the analytical (OLAP) requirements that the stakeholders expect the DWH to fulfill?

[One team member can become a stakeholder temporarily]
column3:
1. Flexible Sales and Demand Planning (what-if queries)
• Net sales and units by month, region, pharmacy, medicine and disease area.
• Physical pharmacy vs e-commerce trend.
• Seasonal demand by disease area.
• What if a promotion runs, or a disease area grows by 20%?

2. Error Predictability and Loss Tracking (net revenue queries)
• Hospital forecast vs actual consumption (forecast error).
• Net revenue, discount and gross margin by medicine and channel.
• Lost demand (unfulfilled packs), stockout days, wastage and returns.

3. Supply and Scenario Planning (what-if queries)
• Requested vs approved vs received quantity per hospital.
• Emergency orders by hospital and medicine.
• What if hospital demand rises, how much more must be produced and stocked?

column1: Use AI to find out more and list all standard analytical requirements which were not specified by stakeholders
column3:
1. Gross-to-Net (GTN) Analysis
• How much of gross sales is lost to discounts and returns.
• GTN gap by payer type (insurance, government, cash, hospital formulary).
• GTN gap by channel, medicine and promotion.

2. Growth and Trend Analysis
• Month-on-month and year-on-year sales growth.
• Weekday vs weekend sales pattern.

3. Product Portfolio Analysis
• ABC (Pareto): which few medicines bring most of the revenue.
• Prescription vs OTC sales split.

4. Forecast Accuracy
• MAPE and forecast bias per hospital and medicine (good MAPE is below 10%).

5. Disease-Driven Demand
• Demand per 1,000 disease cases.
• Hospital size (beds, occupancy) vs medicine consumption.

6. Price and Expiry Analysis
• Discount sensitivity: does a bigger discount sell more units?
• Near-expiry sales: packs sold close to expiry date.

7. Network Performance
• Average sales per pharmacy.
• Fill rate and service level trend over time.

column1: The reason I am building the DWH:
column3: I am building this data warehouse because the company's sales and demand data sit in separate systems, so there is no single view of medicine demand. I want to bring all this data into one place to understand which medicines sell, where, through which channel, and how much hospitals actually need compared to what they forecast. I also want to track inventory on hand at hospitals, and losses like discounts, returns, wastage and unfulfilled demand, and run what-if scenarios. All of this will be shown in dashboards with filters so managers can quickly find answers themselves. This will help the company forecast demand better, avoid stockouts, and plan production and supply on time.
